Fossombronia Fossombroniaceae
 Although this is an easy genus to identify, few species can be identified with certainty
in the field because spore structure is important in- species identification. The plants
usually colonise damp soH in otherwise dry environments. In mallee woodlands they
can form vast sheets, often mixed with Riccia species, in the months after good rains.
The tli.allus consists of a simple stem (usually invisible in the field) from which arise
many thin, leafy, upright or prostrate wings. These wings are often closely packed,
and their margins are usually crinkled and sometimes also lobed, so that many species
resemble miniature lettuces. There is often a tinge of crfmson on the margins, and the
rhizoids are usually crimson (but pale brown to hyaline in some species).
     Of the known species, F intestinalis (WSTVN) is the only one that is easily
r�'cognis-ed in the field. It is a very pale species that commonly forms rows of rosettes,
the wings arranged in neatly overlapping sets.
     F altilameliosa (WSTV) is perhaps the most common species of Fossombronia
in the region. It forms open colonit;s, sometimes tinted with crimson, in dry to wet
f?rest, grassland, woodland and mallee habitats. The shoots are flaccid, commonly
branched once, up to 12 mm long and 2 mm wide. The wings tend to curve inwards to
hide the stem, and those closer to the shoot apex are larger and often 2 or 3-lobed. The
solitary antheridia are protected by the turned-in bases of the wings.
     F pusilla (WSTVAN) grows to about 15 mm long and often forms large, bright
green colonies. The wings are broadly kidney-shaped, and may be shallowly lobed or
entire, and the shoots are often branched. Two varieties- var. pusilla and var. maritima
(= F maritima Paton)- have b�en described; the differences are microscopic.
     F wondraczeckii (WSVN) grows up to 20 mm long and is often branched, but it
usually forms only small colonies. The wings are oblong to almost square, with margins
that vary from entire to trilobed, and plain to very crinkled.
    Austrofossombronia australis (TVA)- Fossombronia naumannii of Scott (1985)-
is·an aquatic or semi aquatic species with rather stiff, kidney-shaped wings that are
often bilebed and deeply crinkled. The �ings and stem towards the base of the plant
are distinctly dark crimson but the wing apices are green and usualiy acutely pointed.

Similar species: Goebelobryum unguil;ulatum, Monocarpus sphaerocarpus, Petalophyllum
preisii, Sphaerocarpos texanus

 Hymenophyton flabellatum Hymenophytaceae                                         TVN
This is one of the commonest bryophytes in wet forest, rainforest and fi;rn gullies. It
forms dense colonies of umbrella-like shoots on living and fallen trees and
tree­ferns, and on rocks in streams. It is espec(ally common close to streams. The
colour is always a pure green, and the vertical stem gives way to a near-perfect circle
of forked horizontal lobes, each with a distinct midrib. The margins of the lobes are
not toothed, unlike th_ose of Symphyogyna podaphylla. Botanists unfamiliar with
liverworts might mistake the shoots for filmy ferns, with which they are often mixed.
   . H. leptopodum (T) is distinguished by its notched frond-tips.

Similar species: P;llavicinia spp., Symphyogyna podophylla, Podomitrium spp.




Lunuiaria cruciata Lunulariaceae                                                 WSTVAN
This species is extremely common on recently disturbed soil and in waste places,
urban gardens and flower-pots. It is probably the most common liverwort world-wide.
Its natural habitat is bare soil on stream banks and moist soil that dries out periodically.
It is usually distinguishable by the presence on the upper surface of crescent-shaped
gemmae j.:ups in which yellow-green, pointed-oval gemmae form. The flat thallus is
divide� into broad lobes and is dotted with whitish pores that lead to air chambers
below. Sporophytes, which are rare, each consist of a stalk supporting four capsules
arranged in a cross (hence cruciata).

Similar species: Marcha�tia spp.
